item.title: MassTransit vs Wolverine vs NServiceBus vs Rebus in 2026: Which .NET Message Bus Survives Production?
item.description: Your first message bus works beautifully in development. Then a consumer throws on a malformed payload at 2 a.m., the message disappears, and nobody can tell you whether it was ever delivered. That is the moment teams discover the difference between a library that sends messages and a framework that owns delivery guarantees. In .NET, four libraries occupy that space — and they disagree fundamentally about how much they should do for you.

item.title: Self-Hosted Message Broker High Availability: RabbitMQ vs Apache Kafka vs NATS Clustering
item.description: When your application depends on asynchronous messaging, a single-node message broker is a ticking time bomb. One server failure and your entire event pipeline grinds to a halt. That’s why production deployments demand high availability (HA) configurations that survive node failures without dropping messages.

item.title: Self-Hosted RabbitMQ Monitoring & Management Dashboards: RabbitMQ Management vs RabbitScout vs rabbitmq_exporter
item.description: RabbitMQ is the most widely deployed open-source message broker, powering asynchronous communication in thousands of production systems. But as your RabbitMQ clusters scale, relying on command-line tools alone becomes impractical. You need visibility into queue depths, consumer health, message rates, and cluster status in real time.
